scenario: AITA for 'stealing' my Dad's business idea and making a success of it? | Title says it all really. I (26M) technically ''stole'' my dad's business idea. When I first heard it from him, it was so simple yet so...genius. I can't say exactly what it is here, but it was genius. The thing is, me and my dad (55M) are complete opposites. He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). Physically, I look more like my grandad, but personality wise, I guess I'm a bit more impulsive and hot headed and not as intelligent as my dad, but I get things done. Perhaps I'm more ''traditional masculine'' than my dad. Its like I should be in the older generation, and he should be from the newer one. When I heard my Dad's business idea, I was amazed, but I didn't truly believe my Dad could pull it off. He doesn't get things done. He's always been full of great ideas, but ideas not put to use are useless. So I took the idea and ran with it. I got IP rights and started the business with it 2 years ago. Since then, its been a massive success. Not millions or anything, but into the six figures and the potential to make millions is there perhaps in the next half decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. Well I confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels and he said I'm a ''fucking asshole''. He said he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. AITA?

The formal attire can signal to your brain that you're in a more serious and important mode, which can boost your confidence and self-assurance. Additionally, wearing a suit and tie can also affect how others perceive you. People may view you as more competent, trustworthy, and authoritative when you're dressed in formal attire. This can lead to a positive feedback loop, where you feel more confident because you're receiving positive cues from others. It's also worth noting that the psychological impact of wearing a suit and tie can be highly personal and subjective. Some people may feel restricted or uncomfortable in formal attire, while others may feel empowered and confident. Ultimately, it's essential to wear what makes you feel good about yourself and helps you project the image you want to convey. So, if wearing a suit and tie makes you feel confident, that's great! prediction.raw: I would say: 1 You are the asshole in this scenario. While it's understandable that you were impressed by your dad's business idea and wanted to bring it to life, taking it without his permission or involvement is a betrayal of his trust. Your dad had shared his idea with you, likely expecting that you would support and help him develop it, not steal it from him. Your justification that your dad is "a man of ideas, but not a man of action" comes across as dismissive and condescending. It's not your place to decide whether your dad is capable of executing his own ideas or not. By taking the idea and running with it, you've not only hurt your dad's feelings but also undermined his confidence and sense of self-worth. Offering your dad 20% of the profits after the fact is not a genuine attempt to make amends, but rather a way to assuage your own guilt. It's too little, too late, and your dad's rejection of the offer is understandable. Your mom and granddad taking your side doesn't necessarily mean you're in the right. Family dynamics can be complex, and it's possible that they're not seeing the full picture or are biased towards you. Ultimately, you should have had an open and honest conversation with your dad about his idea and your desire to help him develop it. You could have offered to partner with him or help him bring the idea to life together. By not doing so, you've damaged your relationship with your dad and caused unnecessary hurt and tension.
